title: Mālinīvijayottaratantra
summary: The root scripture of Abhinavagupta's Trika ('the essence of the Trika', TĀ 1.18). Presented as the teaching given to the sages Sanatkumāra, Nārada, Agastya and others (MVT 1.1-7), it covers emanation and the tattvas, the mālinī order of letters, the three kinds of immersion (āṇava, śākta, śāmbhava; 2.21-23), the five signs of the descent of Rudra's power (2.14-16), initiation and its signs (ānanda, udbhava, kampa, nidrā, ghūrṇi; 11.35), and a long yoga of concentrations on elements, subtle elements and senses (chs. 12-17).

attribution.tradition: Revealed by the Supreme Lord (MVT 1.7: 'issued from the mouth of the Supreme Lord').
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous Vidyāpīṭha tantra, later than the Siddhayogeśvarīmata.

title: Svacchandatantra (Svacchandabhairavatantra)
summary: A principal Mantrapīṭha tantra of the Bhairava corpus, centred on Svacchandabhairava (Aghora) and Aghoreśvarī; the mainstay of Kashmirian Śaiva ritual (worship, initiation), with a large cosmography of the worlds (bhuvanas) and teachings on yoga and the subtle body. Kṣemarāja's Uddyota reads it in the light of non-dual doctrine.

attribution.tradition: Revealed by Bhairava to the Goddess.
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous; widely cited from the 9th c.

title: Netratantra (Mṛtyujidbhaṭṭāraka)
summary: A Bhairava tantra of the cult of Amṛteśvara / Mṛtyuñjit, 'the Eye', whose mantra conquers death. Besides ritual for protection, healing and against possession, it teaches gross, subtle and supreme meditation, the latter two on the subtle body (cakras, ādhāras, lakṣyas, vyomans) and on the formless. Commented on by Kṣemarāja (Netroddyota).

title: Vijñānabhairava
summary: A dialogue in which the Goddess (Bhairavī) asks Bhairava about his true nature; he rejects every form 'with parts' (the ninefold, the mass of sounds, the three-headed, nāda-bindu...) as a device for the confused (vv. 7-13), describes the supreme state as indescribable fullness identical with the Goddess (14-21), and in answer to her request for means (22-23) teaches 112 contemplations (dhāraṇā) of the 'waveless state' (24-138; counted at 139). It then redefines japa, meditation, worship, oblation, sacrifice and bathing as inner acts (144-153), teaches the natural 'haṃsa' repetition of the breath (154-156), enjoins secrecy (157-160), and closes with the Goddess embracing Śiva, having grasped 'the essence of the Rudrayāmala' (161-163).

attribution.tradition: Spoken by Bhairava to Bhairavī; claims to be the essence of the Rudrayāmala and of the Trika (vv. 1, 161-162).
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous. The claimed Rudrayāmala origin cannot be verified: the early Rudrayāmala is lost, and the extant Rudrayāmala (Uttaratantra) is a different and later text. Cited by Kṣemarāja, who began a commentary on it.

scholarly.text: c. 7th-9th c. CE (before Kṣemarāja, c. 1000; uncertain)

structure.description: 163 verses in the numbering of KSTS 8 (with a verse 155b on the haṃsa-japa); 162 in the GRETIL e-text; the Kaumudī recension (KSTS 9) lacks vv. 45 (merged with 44), 84 and 114 and so has exactly 112 verses in its dhāraṇā section. Dhāraṇās: vv. 24-138.

title: Parātrīśikā
summary: A short Kaula-Trika dialogue: the Goddess asks how the Unsurpassed (anuttara) grants immediate Kaula perfection. Bhairava teaches the emanation of the letters as the tattvas (vv. 5-9), the Heart of Bhairava as the 'third Brahman' (10), the powers of reciting and remembering it (11-20), the tattvas from Kālāgni to Śiva (21-23), the universe resting in the Heart-seed as a banyan tree in its seed (24), initiation for one who knows this (25), and a worship procedure (26-33). It closes 'this is the Rudrayāmala' (35).

attribution.tradition: Spoken by Bhairava; presents itself as belonging to the Rudrayāmala (final verse).
attribution.scholarly: Anonymous; transmitted in Kashmir with the commentaries of Abhinavagupta and others.

title: Śivasūtra
summary: Seventy-seven terse aphorisms (Kṣemarāja's recension) on consciousness as the self, bondage as limited knowledge, the states of waking, dream, sleep and the fourth, the powers and pitfalls of yoga, and the life of the realized yogin as a dancer on the stage of the inner self. Kṣemarāja reads its three sections as the śāmbhava, śākta and āṇava means.

attribution.tradition: Revealed by Śiva to Vasugupta: Paramaśiva told him in a dream of a secret on a great rock on Mahādeva mountain, which turned over at his touch (Kṣemarāja, Śivasūtravimarśinī intro.); the sūtras 'appeared by a siddha's command' (Bhāskara, Vārttika 1.3).

structure.description: 3 sections: 22 + 10 + 45 = 77 sūtras in Kṣemarāja's recension (called unmeṣa); 23 + 10 + 46 = 79 in Bhāskara's (called prakāśa): he divides 1.16 in two, adds 3.15 'visargasvābhāvyād abahiḥ sthites tatsthitiḥ', and orders 3.22-23 differently.

title: Spandakārikā
summary: Fifty-odd verses on spanda, the vibrant creative awareness of Śaṅkara: its unobstructed nature and persistence through the states (ch. 1), the identity of mantras and the soul with Śiva (ch. 2), the powers (vibhūti) that come from contact with spanda and the bondage caused by the powers of the mass of sounds when unrecognized (ch. 3).

attribution.tradition: Disputed within the tradition: Kṣemarāja (Spandanirṇaya) holds that Vasugupta composed the verses; Bhāskara (Śivasūtravārttika 1.5: Kallaṭa explained three sections of the Śiva Sūtra 'with his own Spanda-sūtras'), Rāmakaṇṭha and Bhagavadutpala ascribe them to Kallaṭa, conveying Vasugupta's teaching.
attribution.scholarly: Author debated between Vasugupta and Kallaṭa; c. 850-900 CE.

structure.description: Kṣemarāja's recension: 3 niḥṣyandas of 25 + 7 + 19 verses plus 2 concluding verses (53); the recensions of Kallaṭa and Rāmakaṇṭha differ slightly in division and count.

title: Tantrāloka
summary: Abhinavagupta's encyclopaedic exposition of the Trika on the basis of the Mālinīvijayottara, integrating Kaula and Krama. After defining bondage as ignorance and knowledge as the sole cause of liberation (1.22-23), it orders all Śaiva practice by the four means (chs. 2-5), sets out time, space, the tattvas and the paths of manifestation (6-12), the descent of grace (13), the whole ritual of initiation, consecration, funerary and daily rites (14-28), the secret Kula ritual (29), mantra, maṇḍala and mudrā (30-32), and ends with unification, the harmony of the scriptures, the lineage and the author's account of himself (33-37).

structure.description: 37 āhnikas (chapters), c. 5,800 verses; chapter topics per Abhinavagupta's own table of contents (TĀ 1.278-329) and colophons: 1 vijñānabheda (the kinds of knowledge; knowledge as the cause of liberation; table of contents); 2 anupāya (the means-less); 3 śāmbhavopāya (the reflection of the universe in consciousness; the letters); 4 śāktopāya (purification of thought, sattarka, the wheel of consciousness, the twelve Kālīs, critique of rules); 5 āṇavopāya (meditation, uccāra of prāṇa, the seven ānandas, the five signs, karaṇa, varṇa); 6 kālopāya / kālatattva (time in the breath and its cycles); 7 cakrodaya (the arising of the wheels; mantra and breath counts); 8 deśādhvan (the path of space: the worlds); 9 tattvādhvan (the path of the tattvas); 10 tattvabheda (divisions of the tattvas; the states and the seven pramātṛs); 11 kalādhvan (the path of the kalās; letters and mantras); 12 adhvopayoga (use of the paths); 13 śaktipāta (the descent of power; its grades); 14 dīkṣopakrama (preliminaries of initiation; removal of concealment); 15 samayadīkṣā (initiation into the samaya; the samaya rules); 16 prameya (the putraka initiation and the knowables purified); 17 vikṣipta/extended initiation (cord, purification of the tattvas, burning the bonds); 18 saṅkṣiptadīkṣā (abbreviated initiation); 19 sadyaḥsamutkrānti (initiation bringing immediate departure from the body); 20 tulādīkṣā (initiation by the balance); 21 parokṣadīkṣā (initiation of the absent and the dead); 22 liṅgoddhāra (removal of a prior sectarian mark); 23 abhiṣeka (consecration as teacher or adept); 24 antyeṣṭi (final rites); 25 śrāddha (rites for the dead); 26 sthaṇḍilapūjā (daily worship on a ritual ground; the remaining life of the initiate); 27 liṅgārcā (worship of the liṅga); 28 parva-pavitraka etc. (occasional rites; the gathering of yoginīs; rites for the guru); 29 rahasyavidhi (the secret Kula ritual); 30 mantra (the mantras); 31 maṇḍala; 32 mudrā; 33 ekīkāra (unification of the paths); 34 svarūpapraveśa (entry into one's own nature); 35 śāstrasammelana (the harmony of the scriptures); 36 āyātikrama (the descent of the scripture through the lineage); 37 upādeyabhāva (why this scripture is to be accepted; the author's account of himself)
